existing_incident_edges.relationship: centers enslaved people’s agency in the Haitian Revolution
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: A contribution to anti-colonial historical writing, not merely a later recovery project under identity histories. The Black Jacobins makes enslaved revolutionaries historical agents; the argument is not supplied by a generic anti-colonial label.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: reworks Marxist history through Caribbean revolution and popular agency
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Connects distinct Marxist historical projects; does not make James a derivative of postwar British social history. James contributes a Caribbean revolutionary history within Marxist debate, not an example of all anti-colonial histories adopting one theory. The later lectures also reconsider the balance between prominent leaders and popular action. Hobsbawm’s participant memoir explicitly recalls the group reading The Black Jacobins across political differences.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: offers cultural inquiry through cricket, race, colonial society, and life writing
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Primary club descriptions connect color and class with autobiographical choices; the art chapter analyzes cricket’s aesthetic and collective form. This is a methodological contribution to cultural inquiry, not demonstrated influence on Hunt’s collection.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Caribbean historical writing and London Marxist study inform Rodney’s formation
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: West’s assessment identifies The Black Jacobins. The Foundation names C. L. R. and Selma James in London study; James’s 1981 retrospective locates Rodney within a Caribbean intellectual inheritance. These sources support formation but not agreement on strategy or every textual debt.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: provides materialist resources reworked in histories of slavery and revolution
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Retargeted from the anti-colonial umbrella to James. The feedback’s blanket assertion that both James and Eric Williams write as Marxists is not adopted; their distinct arguments remain visible. James’s 1971 recollection names his reading of Trotsky, Lenin and Marx. It supports a specific resource while leaving exact retrospective chronology open; Williams is not assigned the same theoretical identity.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: James criticizes Rodney’s political preparation for taking power
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: The 1981 memorial lecture offers a strategic disagreement alongside admiration. James’s diagnosis is not adopted as an explanation of the assassination or proof of what Rodney did not know. This differs from the formative influence in edge_156.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: James’s later comparison takes up Du Bois on popular political imagination
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: The 1971 lecture praises Black Reconstruction’s treatment of participants’ ideas. This is documented later engagement, not a claim that Du Bois supplied James’s original 1938 argument.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: James revisits revolutionary history through ordinary participants
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: His 1971 lecture proposes expanding research into local leaders beyond his earlier narration. This is a historical-method contribution, not institutional membership or evidence that every suggested revision became a published book.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Haitian revolution joins Caribbean and European revolutionary histories
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: The Black Jacobins supplies an earlier regional contribution to later Atlantic inquiry. The edge marks subject and explanation, not proof that a single later Atlantic school descended from James.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: The Black Jacobins as a model for analysing “metropole and colony in one lens” (2003)
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Her own acknowledgement, read by the second research pass (JBS 42:4, 2003, p. 533): "Colonizers were made both in the metropole and on colonial sites. And, as C. L. R. James's The Black Jacobins (1938) taught us, much can be gained through the analysis of metropole and colony in one lens." A retrospective acknowledgement made in defending the book's method; it names a resource, not the origin of her project. Her 2014 essay also sets James and Williams against the British Marxist pantheon (History Workshop Journal 78, p. 23, read).
existing_incident_edges.map_label: Metropole and colony in one lens, 2003

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Credits James’s historical and dialectical writings as formative resources for his own historical thinking.
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Kelley names The Black Jacobins among his formative historical models and separately identifies Notes on Dialectics, Spheres of Existence and Facing Reality. He expressly preserves Grace Lee Boggs and Cornelius Castoriadis’s coauthorship of Facing Reality. Specific historical and methodological uses are consolidated; original James books remain unread.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Brundage compares Race Rebels with Beyond a Boundary for their accounts of marginalized people’s cultural creativity and agency.
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: The signed review opening explicitly compares the two books’ bold yet nuanced methods and attention to rebellious inventiveness. This is Brundage’s bounded comparison, not his proof that Beyond a Boundary caused Race Rebels or that every argument is identical. Kelley’s own stated use of other James works is separately sourced. Original books remain unread.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Scott compares Mintz and James on plantation slavery’s coercive production of modern social relations.
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Scott 2004, 202/n36 explicitly compares their accounts of discipline, temporality and social change, without excusing violence or reducing either to an identical whole historiography. Undirected named mediation, not proof of direct reading, formal teaching or personal reply. James 1963 appendix and Mintz 1996 complete originals unread.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Cooper uses James’s account of exploitation and transatlantic revolutionary mobilization to connect labour organization with political ideas across empires.
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own 2000:63/note 7 at 68 attributes to James both the organization of Caribbean plantation labour and the movement of revolutionary news and claims. The note cites The Black Jacobins in its 1963 edition while the prose dates the original argument 1938. Cooper places Trouillot’s qualification beside James’s account; this is an argumentative use, not fresh reading or independent verification of James’s historical claims.

named_group_routes.relationship: James, Williams and Césaire challenge different imperial historical narratives
named_group_routes.evidence_note: James, Williams, and Rodney challenge different imperial narratives; national liberation is not a single explanatory position. Césaire’s checked opening attacks civilizing claims; Williams’s economic propositions remain disputed.

named_group_routes.relationship: shares diasporic and emancipatory arguments
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Diasporic and emancipatory concerns intersect, without making all Black and anti-colonial histories one school.

named_group_routes.relationship: James’s changing historical and dramatic work recasts Marxist questions through enslaved revolution
named_group_routes.evidence_note: The earlier wording grouped James and Williams too closely under Marxist social history. Individual entries now distinguish their arguments. James is a specified participant who recasts Marxist historical questions through slavery and revolution. Not all anti-colonial thinkers share that position. Douglas’s publisher description supplies edition-specific support, not a single Marxist identity for the umbrella.
named_group_routes.map_label: James: revolution and changing Marxist questions

named_group_routes.relationship: James and Williams examine slavery and revolution across imperial boundaries
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Earlier transregional scholarship is not retrospectively assigned a single later Atlantic-school identity. Gilroy’s preface acknowledges limited treatment of James and Fanon; it cannot substantiate detailed reception of either. The separately recorded James/Williams contributions retain their own evidence.

named_group_routes.relationship: places women’s rights organizing alongside labor and Black women’s activity before the 1960s
named_group_routes.evidence_note: James and Rupp identify broader coverage while offering different criticisms. Later women’s history is neither a uniform continuation nor a field founded by this book alone. Original 1959 text and later editions remain distinct.
named_group_routes.map_label: Rights organizing, labor and archival reach

named_group_routes.relationship: Frances James asks for a structural explanation through private property and a program beyond reform
named_group_routes.evidence_note: The 1960 review also welcomes labor and Black women’s coverage. This particular Marxist criticism does not make the book devoid of explanation, identify James with Janet Wilson James or establish a uniform Marxist response.

named_group_routes.relationship: Environmental change through land use, subsistence and labour: Island County (1980), the roots of Native dependency (1983) and the Columbia as an organic machine (1995), with an early survey of the field (1985)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: White's own statements, known for his books only through Google Books search-within snippets (page images not seen) and therefore paraphrased where the wording carries the claim. Land Use, Environment, and Social Change (1980; snippets of the 1992 paperback, whose body text is the 1980 text; p. 7 as given in the snippet results): White presents the book as departing somewhat from recent environmental history, which he describes as mostly a variant of intellectual and political history, by tracing the environmental impact of Indian and later intruding peoples and its consequences for their societies; on the same page he credits James Malin's Great Plains studies, ignored by most historians, as a trail to follow. In the preface to the 1992 edition (November 1991; snippet, folio xviii inferred from Google Books page ids that carry the printed folios xi, xvi and xvii) he judges his own use of ecology: 'I used ecological concepts like community, succession, climax, and ecosystem unproblematically even though within the discipline of ecology those ideas had already come under attack'. Cronon's foreword (October 1991; snippets, folio xi observed) places the book among White's contributions 'to environmental history, to the history of the American West, to Indian history, and to American history generally' and calls it 'a textbook case of an underappreciated classic' (p. xi). The Organic Machine (1995; snippets of the preface, whose printed folios were not visible, and of the conclusion, p. 112 taken from the Google Books page id, not seen as a printed folio), in paraphrase: White examines the Columbia as an organic machine, an energy system modified by human intervention that keeps natural, unmade qualities; human labour is energy as much as the river's flow or the calories salmon store for their journey; environmentalists, he argues, distance humans from nature by favouring the eye over the hand and contemplation over work; and the conclusion finds the nature in us in our labour and energy (p. 112). In-period third-party readings: Cronon (1993; OCR of the author-hosted page scan) footnotes Land Use and The Roots of Dependency (nn. 15, 23) for the lesson that 'the horse was not simply a European invader, but a complex cultural entity' (p. 9); D. R. Miller (1994; PDF read in full) calls him 'The social and environmental historian Richard White' (p. 157) and quotes The Middle Ground that dependency 'is an economic, political, and social relationship, but can also be an environmental relationship' (p. 169). On the 1985 survey (unread; paywalled): Worster (1990, read in the 2002–03 Portuguese translation, n. 5, p. 42) calls it the best effort to trace the field's emergence, 'pelo menos em uma parte influente do mundo', reporting White's view that frontier and western history was the formative influence; Cronon's 1994 graduate syllabus assigns it 'read for main themes' (p. 4); in Canada, Cook (1990) cites it (n. 4) for Turner and Webb as 'important, if declining, influences into the 1950s' (p. 6). A contribution, not a founding. Later readings, not evidence for this edge: Isenberg (2013) names White among historians who 'synthesized the material and cultural approaches to the environment' (p. 87) and quotes his 1990 round-table objection that Worster's scheme reduced culture to 'superstructure in the old vulgar Marxist sense' (pp. 88–89, citing JAH 76, pp. 1112–1113; the JAH text is unread).
named_group_routes.map_label: Land use, labour and the field, 1980–1995

named_group_routes.relationship: Orientalism as discourse and as a style of domination: Western knowledge and representation of 'the Orient' read through knowledge and power, extended to contrapuntal reading of the metropolitan canon with empire (1978–93)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: His own in-period statements. Orientalism (New York: Pantheon, 1978, first edition; page images checked): 'The Orient was almost a European invention' (p. 1); Orientalism as 'a style of thought based upon an ontological and epistemological distinction made between "the Orient" and (most of the time) "the Occident"' (p. 2) and as 'a Western style for dominating, restructuring, and having authority over the Orient' (p. 3). He qualifies it at once: 'it would be wrong to conclude that the Orient was essentially an idea, or a creation with no corresponding reality'; 'The relationship between Occident and Orient is a relationship of power, of domination, of varying degrees of a complex hegemony' (p. 5); and he leaves open 'how one can study other cultures and peoples from a libertarian, or a nonrepressive and nonmanipulative, perspective. But then one would have to rethink the whole complex problem of knowledge and power' (p. 24). Covering Islam (1981, introduction, p. ix): 'The underlying theme of Orientalism is the affiliation of knowledge with power.' 'Orientalism Reconsidered', Cultural Critique 1 (1985), read in full: the issues are 'the representation of other cultures, societies, histories; the relationship between power and knowledge' (p. 89); 'what for the most part got left out of Orientalism was precisely the very history that resisted its ideological as well as political encroachments' (p. 94); 'Orientalism is a praxis of the same sort, albeit in different territories, as male gender dominance, or patriarchy' (p. 103). Culture and Imperialism (New York: Knopf, 1993, first edition): 'What I left out of Orientalism was that response to Western dominance which culminated in the great movement of decolonization' (p. xii); 'we begin to reread it not univocally but contrapuntally, with a simultaneous awareness both of the metropolitan history that is narrated and of those other histories against which (and together with which) the dominating discourse acts' (p. 51); 'contrapuntal reading must take account of both processes, that of imperialism and that of resistance to it' (p. 66). In-period reception and criticism. Bernard Lewis, 'The Question of Orientalism', New York Review of Books, 24 June 1982 (web text, read in full, no page numbers): 'To prove this point, Mr. Said makes a number of very arbitrary decisions. His Orient is reduced to the Middle East, and his Middle East to a part of the Arab world'; 'a history of Arabic studies in Europe without the Germans makes as much sense as would a history of European music or philosophy with the same omission'; 'The most rigorous and penetrating critique of Orientalist scholarship has always been and will remain that of the Orientalists themselves.' Said's reply (NYRB, 12 August 1982): 'It is idiotic to say that Orientalism is a conspiracy or to suggest that "the West" is evil', while its 'modern discourse is correctly perceived as a discourse of power'; Lewis answered that 'It is difficult to argue with a scream of rage' and that the book 'takes a genuine problem of real importance, and reduces it to the level of political polemic and personal abuse'. Sadik Jalal al-'Azm, 'Orientalism and Orientalism in Reverse', Khamsin 8 (1981) (web text, read in full) credits 'laying bare Orientalism's persistent belief that there exists a radical ontological difference' between Orient and Occident, but holds that tracing Orientalism back to Homer 'simply lends strength to the essentialistic categories of "Orient" and "Occident"'. Rosalind O'Hanlon and David Washbrook (CSSH 1992; first-page extract only, as recorded in its source note) call Said's blend of themes 'virtually a paradigm for a new generation of historians and anthropologists' in Indian colonial history. Cheryl McEwan, Journal of Historical Geography 22 (1996), read in full: 'The inspiration behind the critical interest in empire, knowledge and power was undoubtedly Edward Said's groundbreaking and provocative Orientalism' (p. 489); feminist scholars 'argue that the critics of Orientalism and ethnocentric scholarship continue to write out gender' (p. 489); Reina Lewis's Gendering Orientalism (1996) is 'a response to Said in its efforts to destabilize the homogenizing tendencies of twentieth-century critiques of Orientalism' (p. 490). Said answered Dennis Porter's charge that he is 'ahistorical and inconsistent' as 'more weighty in assertion than it is in proof' (1985, p. 90); Porter's essay (1983) was not read. Not read: James Clifford's review essay (History and Theory 19, 1980) and Lata Mani and Ruth Frankenberg, 'The Challenge of Orientalism' (Economy and Society 14, 1985); both are recorded as metadata only. Later reading, labelled: Robert Irwin (2006, p. 299) writes that 'Early reviews of Orientalism were mostly hostile'. A contribution to postcolonial critique; the evidence does not make him its founder. edge_107 (language → post), edge_419 (post → indigenous) and edge_693 (post → geography) name him as a resource for others and stay.

named_group_routes.relationship: Culture and Imperialism's account of resistance culture: anticolonial histories such as James's The Black Jacobins and Antonius's The Arab Awakening read as a 'voyage in' to metropolitan culture, alongside post-independence critiques by Guha and Alatas (1993)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: His own in-period text. Culture and Imperialism (Knopf, 1993), chapter 3, 'Resistance and Opposition'. He distinguishes liberal anti-colonialism, which did 'not dispute the fundamental superiority of Western man', from anti-imperialism, and argues 'there was no overall condemnation of imperialism until—and this is my point—after native uprisings were too far gone to be ignored or defeated' (pp. 240–241). Anti-imperialist work by writers from the peripheries in the metropolis is 'usually an extension into the metropolis of large-scale mass movements'; 'There is thus an overlap and interdependence that cannot theoretically be described as only the reactive assertion of a separate colonial or native identity'; 'The voyage in, then, constitutes an especially interesting variety of hybrid cultural work' (p. 244). He reads 'C.L.R. James's The Black Jacobins, published in 1938, and, appearing at almost the same time, George Antonius's The Arab Awakening' as works 'intended as serious works of scholarship and advocacy addressed from within a national movement for independence to a general audience', set against Ranajit Guha's A Rule of Property for Bengal (1963) and S. H. Alatas's The Myth of the Lazy Native (1977), which are 'post-colonial and specialist' (p. 245); 'history for Guha is critique, not the dutiful replication of colonialist objects, ideologies, and arguments' (p. 251). He also treats Fanon as one who 'programmatically seeks to treat colonial and metropolitan societies together' (p. 278). The introduction frames the chapter: 'What I left out of Orientalism was that response to Western dominance which culminated in the great movement of decolonization' (p. xii). Read: pp. xii, 240–245, 251, 278; the rest of the chapter (including the Fanon and Cabral sections) was not read closely. No in-period review assessing this chapter for historians was read. A contribution to how anticolonial histories are read and placed, not a claim that he wrote anticolonial history in their sense; The Question of Palestine (1979) is mentioned in the node, not used for this edge.
named_group_routes.map_label: Resistance culture and the voyage in, 1993

named_group_routes.relationship: Mixed-race relationships not to be explained by white women's absence: Perry's 1995 criticism of fur-trade historians, Van Kirk's 'brilliant account' included, for treating intermarriage as the product of that absence, and her 2001 argument (as Carter reports it) that such relationships were 'not confined to the fur trade' and that 'happy stories' of fur-trade marriages can 'obscure both coercive details and the larger brutality of colonialism'
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own words, in period. 1995 (BC Studies 105/106, read at p. 30): 'Historians of the fur trade, while concerned with establishing the salience of mixed-race relationships, nonetheless explain their frequency as the product of white women's absence'; n. 8: 'For a brilliant account which ultimately suggests that the existence of mixed-race relationships was the result of white women's absence from the fur trade, see Sylvia Van Kirk, "Many Tender Ties" … Also see Jennifer S. H. Brown, Strangers in Blood … and Robin Fisher, Contact and Conflict'; n. 11 quotes Van Kirk: 'Had it been possible for fur traders to bring their wives out at an earlier date, it is doubtful whether intermarriage with native women would have been so extensive' (Many Tender Ties, p. 173); the 'volcano theory' 'holds that mixed-race relationships are at worst unfathomable and at best the products of abnormal historical circumstances' (p. 30). Qualifications kept: the criticism is of one explanation, not of the field; she calls Van Kirk's account 'brilliant' (p. 30 n. 8) and 'pioneering' (p. 43), and relies on it for the displacement of Aboriginal women (p. 43). 2001: the book is unread; Carter (BC Studies 136, p. 118, read) reports that 'Perry does not write a history of these relationships, noting the difficulties with available sources, but she does argue that they were not confined to the fur trade and could be found in the city, in the country, and in mining towns', and that she 'stresses the need to look beyond the "happy stories," such as the long marriage of James Douglas and Amelia Connolly, that can "obscure both coercive details and the larger brutality of colonialism" (62)'. In-period counterpoint: Orlowski (2002, p. 121, read) faults the book because 'the mixed-race couples in colonial B.C. had much to do with building alliances, sometimes between Hudson's Bay Company officers and the daughters of Aboriginal chiefs, a strategy that is not considered at all in the book'. No reply by Van Kirk or Brown was checked. Later reading, labelled: in 2016 (p. 113) she proposes thinking 'seriously about fur-trade colonialism as a distinct and meaningful practice of empire' (Colonial Relations, on the Douglas–Connolly family, is unread). Target: Van Kirk's person entry, since the criticism is of her explanation of intermarriage; her entry cites Perry's 2008 essay on her work only as a later reading.
named_group_routes.map_label: Perry: mixed-race unions beyond white women's absence, 1995–2001

named_group_routes.relationship: Williams’s Capitalism and Slavery tested on the compensation records: supported on slave-wealth in British society, qualified on decline, and set against a British Marxist pantheon that left James and Williams out (2009–2014)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own words, read (History Workshop Journal 78, 2014). "C. L. R James and Eric Williams did not appear in their pantheon. James and Williams, in their struggle against racism and colonialism insisted on the linkage between metropole and colony … the intimate connections … between capitalism and slavery" (p. 23). "Williams never argued that slavery 'caused' the Industrial Revolution … as Nicholas Draper, Keith McClelland and I suggest in the co-authored book which documents the results of the first phase of our project on the Legacies of British Slave-Ownership (LBS), there is a move to a modified version of Williams’s thesis amongst economic historians" (p. 24); "Williams’s insight into the importance of slave-derived wealth to eighteenth-century society and culture has been greatly expanded" (p. 24). Qualifications: the modified thesis is attributed jointly to the LBS authors and set among economic historians (Pomeranz, Inikori); it is not a claim that slavery caused industrialization. The jointly written introduction to Legacies of British Slave-ownership (2014; read in part by the second research pass, without print pages) tests Williams directly: "Eric Williams' Capitalism and Slavery included four connected arguments that are critical for us"; "our findings are entirely supportive of Williams in the context of this second thesis" (slave-wealth in British society); on industrialisation "Our material cannot resolve these controversies"; and the work "complicates Williams by qualifying his 'decline' thesis". Katie Donington, a co-author, recalls that "The project foregrounded Williams's work" (Black Perspectives, 2020). Hall was the project's principal investigator (REF 2014 case study).

named_group_routes.relationship: Carried the linguistic turn into political history: between the Reform Acts 'the official political subject was redefined in the image of print' (1993, as quoted by Tilly); asked 'Who's Afraid of the "Linguistic Turn"?' (1994); gathered the new political history in Re-reading the Constitution (1996)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Politics and the People pp. 107 and 336 as quoted by Tilly (1994, read in full; the book unread): 'this period witnessed a marked decline in people's ability to shape the political appeals available to them as the official political subject was redefined in the image of print'; 'The invention of democracy in England was then a sham'. The 1994 Social History article is unread; its title and subtitle answer Mayfield and Thorne (1992). Re-reading the Constitution: contents read. Eley and Nield (2000, p. 8, read): 'James Vernon eschews the normal ground of political history' for 'neglected traces like ballads, banners, cartoons, handbills, statues, architecture'. Drafting addition built from agent B's evidence (§§B1–B3, P5).

named_group_routes.relationship: Thapar challenges colonial and religious-nationalist divisions of India’s past in her 2015 keynote
named_group_routes.evidence_note: The speech criticizes the Hindu/Muslim partition of historical time inherited from James Mill and tests the Somanatha trauma narrative against differing sources. This targets specified narratives, not every national history.
named_group_routes.map_label: Thapar challenges colonial and religious-nationalist divisions of India’s past in her 2015 keynote

named_group_routes.relationship: Higginbotham explicitly uses Scott’s infrapolitics for her discussion of micropolitical resistance (1992).
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Her note 67 identifies Domination and the Arts of Resistance, pp183–192; James C. Scott is distinct from Joan W. Scott.

named_group_routes.relationship: Gilroy identifies Du Bois’s double consciousness as a central organizing resource for his inquiry into the Black Atlantic.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: The Black Atlantic, preface p. x, visually checked after OCR reading of ix–xi. This is Gilroy’s explicit acknowledgment, not an inference from a subtitle. Chapter 4 and the Du Bois originals were not reread; the book’s provisional, anti-closure framework and scant treatment of Fanon and James remain qualified.

named_group_routes.relationship: Higginbotham places Scott’s language-and-discourse turn among feminist frameworks she found compelling but insufficiently attentive to race.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Her 2017 retrospective, printed p.632, names Scott’s 1986 article and 1988 book before explaining her qualified dissatisfaction with feminist theory’s racial presumptions. The criticism concerns a wider body of theory, with Scott a named example, not Scott alone. This is Higginbotham’s retrospective account of the context of her 1992 intervention, not evidence of a private exchange, a 1992 direct denunciation or rejection of every Scott argument. James C.Scott’s separate infrapolitics resource is a different person.

named_group_routes.relationship: As Catherine Hall reports, Bayly criticizes James Scott for overstating state authority and relying too heavily on official records.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Explicit Hall mediation: her full archived review paragraph on state and society names James Scott separately from users of Foucault. The original book passage and Scott’s works remain unread here. This particular criticism does not establish rejection of all Scott’s scholarship or identify him with Joan Scott.

named_group_routes.relationship: Calloway draws on White’s account of negotiated Native power and cultural accommodation to unsettle an English-centered, east-to-west account of early America.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own 2011 interview explains the particular resource; Parmenter 1999 p124 separately identifies White alongside James Axtell and James Merrell in New Worlds for All. Their credit remains plural. Bailyn 1995 also names White’s resource in Calloway’s Revolution book. These are distinct witnesses, consolidated in one contribution claim. The complete books and Calloway’s 1992 review remain unread.

named_group_routes.relationship: Richter praises Bailyn’s colonial synthesis but challenges language and interpretation that minimize Native settlement, strategic choice and power in shaping colonial migration.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own Harvard Magazine review online 14 December 2012/print January–February 2013. The objection concerns The Barbarous Years and its peopling framework, not every Bailyn work. Richter explicitly credits James Merrell’s language critique and uses Francis Jennings and Cynthia Van Zandt for the Susquehannock example; retain their credit without inventing endpoints. Praise and disagreement coexist. Bailyn’s full book and any reply remain unread; the apparent PDF link redirects to an accessibility notice, so no print-page collation is claimed.

named_group_routes.relationship: Armitage credits conversations with Iriye and other international historians with helping crystallize his turn toward international and global history.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own 2012 retrospective singles out the 2000/1 Warren Center conversations and jointly credits Ernest May and James Kloppenberg. The resource is this intellectual exchange, not an unspecified Iriye book or sole conversion cause. It coexisted with Atlantic work.

named_group_routes.relationship: Armitage and Guldi present James C. Scott’s Zomia history as an example of combining local histories into an account that challenges inevitable state and economic development.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Joint 2014 conclusion makes this specific methodological use of The Art of Not Being Governed 2009. Scott’s historical claims are reported as their reading, not independently verified; no all-purpose influence or agreement is inferred. Original book unread.

named_group_routes.relationship: Uses Roediger’s whiteness studies among resources for relating immigrant ethnicity, class and racial formation.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: The 1999 article, p. 70 and note 9, cites Barrett and Roediger's joint Inbetween Peoples and Roediger's Towards the Abolition of Whiteness. The 2014 foreword, p. xxiii and note 4, calls critical race and working class scholarship influential, listing The Wages of Whiteness and the joint essay among examples. James Barrett and other contributors retain credit. The later retrospective is not treated as the cause of the 2004 book; originals remain unread.

named_group_routes.relationship: Cites Making a New Deal among studies relating immigrant assimilation to twentieth-century class formation.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: The 1999 article, p. 70 and note 9, identifies Cohen's 1990 study as an example of the specified historiographical approach, alongside Gerstle and James Barrett. This is a bounded textual reference, not formal mentorship, an exclusive framework or agreement with the whole book. Cohen's original remains unread.

named_group_routes.relationship: Names Rodney’s How Europe Underdeveloped Africa as a model that drew him toward historical and revolutionary study.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: In his own named-resources answer, Kelley describes Rodney’s book as opening dependency/underdevelopment literature, then places it with Du Bois and James among three formative historical texts. Samir Amin and Andre Gunder Frank retain credit in that pathway. Original Rodney book remains unread for this dossier; retrospective self-report is not an exclusive genealogy.

named_group_routes.relationship: Credits Black Reconstruction as one of the formative historical models that drew him into the discipline.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Kelley explicitly names Du Bois’s book alongside James’s Black Jacobins and Rodney’s How Europe Underdeveloped Africa. The three are co-credited; this is stronger than a shared Black-history topic or bibliographic mention. The original Du Bois book remains unread here.

named_group_routes.relationship: Names Selections from the Prison Notebooks among the Marxist works that shaped his historical thinking.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: His own answer singles out Gramsci and that work among chief authors/texts, while crediting Luxemburg, James, the Boggses and many others. It establishes an explicit resource without assigning every use of organic intellectuals exclusively to Gramsci: Kelley separately credits Lipsitz’s concrete framework. Original Prison Notebooks remains unread.

named_group_routes.relationship: Judges James Walker's survey of Canadian historical writing about Indigenous peoples 'eye-opening' but 'conservative and inadequate': 'Canadian historiography is not that benign' (1999)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own words, dissertation (University of Manitoba, 1999), PDF p. 119, read by Agent B (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-indigenous-authored.md §1.7): 'I find James Walker's assessment of Canadian historical writing conservative and inadequate.
